seats.oldValue: Dust, which had got into his throat and eyes.
seats.newValue: Dust, which was in his throat and eyes.
seats.execution: Line 3 puts the dust 'in his throat and eyes'. That is true inside the window, but it is the wrong element: lines 3 to 4 say it was 'splashes of whitewash' that were 'all over his black fur'.

seats.oldValue: His back and arms hurt too much to go on.
seats.newValue: He was so tired and sore that he could not go on.
seats.execution: He is tired and sore, with 'an aching back and weary arms' (line 4), but lines 5 to 9 give the cause as spring's 'spirit of divine discontent and longing' and 'Something up above was calling him'. He bolts out and then digs hard up the tunnel, so he could go on; the body is offered where the text signals a feeling.

seats.oldValue: To show the Mole was bored and fed up with the climb.
seats.newValue: To show the Mole was bored, and fed up with hard work.
seats.execution: A dismissive reading of the repetition. Lines 11 to 14 show him 'working busily' and cheering himself on with 'Up we go! Up we go!', which is effort, not boredom; the piled-up digging verbs make the climb feel long and hard.

seats.oldValue: At the gap in the hedge.
seats.newValue: At the gap in the hedge, far across the meadow.
seats.execution: The gap and the hedge come at lines 21 to 22, after he has crossed the meadow 'till he reached the hedge on the further side'. Lines 14 to 15 put him 'rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow'.

seats.oldValue: The birds were much louder than usual that day.
seats.newValue: The birds were shouting at him because they did not want him in the meadow.
seats.execution: Line 19 says the song fell on his hearing 'almost like a shout', a comparison, not real shouting. Line 18 calls it 'the carol of happy birds', so nothing in the text makes them hostile; the loudness comes from his 'dulled hearing' after the cellarage.

seats.oldValue: He is rushing home to get his dinner.
seats.newValue: He is rushing home because he has not had his dinner yet.
seats.execution: No dinner and no journey home appear in lines 23 to 27; 'Onion-sauce!' is a jeer at the rabbits, not a meal, and line 28 has him meandering 'aimlessly' away. The motive is invented to explain his hurry.

seats.oldValue: Because the river was dangerous and might grab the Mole.
seats.newValue: Because the river was dangerous, as it might grab the Mole.
seats.execution: Pulls the gripping in line 30 to its most threatening reading. Lines 30 to 31 have the river 'chuckling', leaving things 'with a laugh' and finding 'fresh playmates', so it is playful, not a danger to the Mole.

seats.oldValue: The Mole could not keep up with the river.
seats.newValue: The Mole was too small and slow to keep up with the river.
seats.execution: Takes 'when very small' from the comparison in line 34 as a fact about the Mole. The words 'very small' belong to the child walking beside the storyteller; the Mole himself 'trotted' beside the river and kept with it, held 'spell-bound' (line 35) as the child is.

seats.oldValue: To show that the Mole was creeping closer with every step.
seats.newValue: To show the Mole was creeping up to the hole, one small step at a time.
seats.execution: Line 39 has the Mole sitting: 'As he sat on the grass and looked across the river', and the hole is in 'the bank opposite' (line 39). He does not move; only the face appears, one detail per line, as lines 48 to 52 show.

seats.oldValue: He slipped past her, glancing at her as he went.
seats.newValue: He looked at her quickly as he slipped past.
seats.execution: Differs from the text by one detail: lines 5 to 6 say he went past her 'without looking at her', and line 6 adds 'Had he looked'. The quickness is right ('as quickly as possible'); the looking is the reverse of the text.

seats.oldValue: She took the girl into her charge from him.
seats.newValue: She came off the train and took charge of the girl from him.
seats.execution: Line 20 is right that she 'came off the train with that girl', but lines 20 to 21 say she 'gave her into my charge'. The giving is reversed: the stationmaster took charge of the girl from Mrs Spencer.

seats.oldValue: She stands up and holds out both her hands.
seats.newValue: She stands up, grasping the handle of her bag with both hands.
seats.execution: One detail differs: lines 48 to 49 say she grasps the bag 'with one thin brown hand' and 'the other she held out to him'. Both hands on the bag leaves nothing held out.

seats.oldValue: He never makes a decision by himself.
seats.newValue: He is a man who never makes a decision by himself.
seats.execution: An absolute the text refutes: lines 59 to 60 say 'then and there he decided what to do', and the decision is his own. Handing the telling to Marilla (line 61) is one choice, not proof that he never decides.

seats.oldValue: Come along with him, and carry her own bag.
seats.newValue: Come along with him, and take her own bag.
seats.execution: Right on 'Come along' (line 64) and wrong on one detail: lines 64 to 65 end 'Give me your bag', so Matthew asks to take the bag himself, not for her to keep it.

seats.oldValue: It was slow, so the journey felt easy.
seats.newValue: The cart was heavy, and its wheels ran along pleasantly.
seats.execution: Differs from the text by one word: line 3 says 'it was so light'. The wheels running along 'so pleasantly' are right, so a child matching on gist takes it; heavy is the reverse of the reason Beauty gives.

seats.oldValue: It was falling now that the rain had stopped.
seats.newValue: It was low, and he feared a bad night.
seats.execution: The man said 'the river was rising fast' (line 10). Low belongs to the road in line 11, 'one low part of the road', and has been moved onto the river.

seats.oldValue: A shower of dry leaves blown across the road.
seats.newValue: Other trees came crashing down around the oak.
seats.execution: Line 23 reads 'crashing down among the other trees came an oak'. The oak is what fell; the other trees are where it fell. This swaps them, making the other trees fall around the oak.

seats.oldValue: The dog-cart was too heavy to turn on the road.
seats.newValue: The dog-cart was too heavy, so he could not turn it round.
seats.execution: Nothing in lines 24 to 26 is about the weight of the cart, and line 3 calls the dog-cart 'so light'. Beauty gives his own reason in line 26: 'I was not brought up to that'.

seats.oldValue: Drive slowly over the tree where it lay lowest.
seats.newValue: Drive round the tree, then on to the wooden bridge.
seats.execution: Line 29 says 'we can't drive over that tree, nor yet get round it'. Dropping the 'nor' turns the plan into going round the tree, where John's actual plan is 'to go back to the four crossways' (line 30).

seats.oldValue: That the gatekeeper was to blame for the broken bridge.
seats.newValue: That Beauty could not understand much of what they said.
seats.execution: True inside the window: line 54 has Beauty say 'I could not understand much of what they said'. It is the wrong element; what master and John worked out follows in lines 55 to 58, that they would 'all have been drowned'.

seats.oldValue: That Beauty repeats the words to show off what he knows.
seats.newValue: That Beauty repeats their words to show off, and prove how much he understands.
seats.execution: An invented motive, and the reverse of what the lines keep saying. Line 41 has 'Of course I could not tell him' and line 54 'I could not understand much of what they said'.

seats.oldValue: Jane could feel the cold through her muff.
seats.newValue: Jane could feel the cold in her hands.
seats.execution: Line 3 says 'I did not feel the cold', with her hands sheltered 'in my muff'. Dropping the 'not' turns the line round; the cold is shown by the 'sheet of ice covering the causeway' (line 4).

seats.oldValue: She was afraid of the horse in the dusk.
seats.newValue: In the dusk, she was afraid of the horse.
seats.execution: Lines 10 to 11 give the reason outright: 'as the path was narrow, I sat still to let it go by'. Fear is not stated there; she was 'just leaving the stile' (line 10) and stayed only to let the horse pass.

seats.oldValue: She had seen a Gytrash on this lane before.
seats.newValue: A dog was coming upon her in the dusk, as in Bessie's tales.
seats.execution: The dog is real but comes later: it glides out at line 20. The Gytrash comes into her mind at lines 14 to 18, 'As this horse approached', before any dog has appeared.

seats.oldValue: Its black and white colour stood out against the trees.
seats.newValue: It was exactly one form of Bessie's Gytrash, with a huge head.
seats.execution: True inside the window (lines 21 to 22), but it is why the dog looked like a Gytrash, not what showed her it was not one. That is the rider in lines 24 to 26: 'The man, the human being, broke the spell at once.'

seats.oldValue: The exclamation the rider made as he went down on the road.
seats.newValue: A sliding sound, an exclamation and then a clattering tumble.
seats.execution: All three are in lines 27 to 28, but they are what Jane heard as the fall happened, not what caused it. The cause is in lines 28 to 29: 'they had slipped on the sheet of ice'.

seats.oldValue: He has broken a bone in his foot.
seats.newValue: A sprain, and some broken bones in his foot.
seats.execution: Line 49 says 'I have no broken bones,—only a sprain'. The sprain is right; dropping the 'no' adds broken bones he says he does not have.

seats.oldValue: He grew rich first, but then he gave up buying the boys.
seats.newValue: He grew rich first, but then he could not buy the boys.
seats.execution: The order is reversed. His goods could not buy freedom at lines 4 to 7, in the morning; he is 'rolling in wealth' only by 'the middle of the afternoon' (lines 60 to 61).

seats.oldValue: He begins to feel sorry for Tom.
seats.newValue: He begins to feel very sorry for Tom.
seats.execution: Lines 34 to 37 show interest, not pity: Ben stops 'nibbling his apple' and watches 'every move', 'getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed'.

seats.oldValue: A newspaper he had brought in with him.
seats.newValue: A newspaper that he had brought in with him.
seats.execution: No newspaper appears in lines 1 to 5. Line 4 has him ask about 'The Pickwick Papers', which lines 4 to 5 say were 'then publishing in parts'; the word papers makes a newspaper sound likely.

seats.oldValue: Her father was the rector of the town.
seats.newValue: She was the daughter of a rector of Cranford.
seats.execution: True of her (line 6), but it is not the cause the text gives. Lines 6 to 8 say she 'considered herself literary' 'on the strength of a number of manuscript sermons, and a pretty good library of divinity'.

seats.oldValue: At first she has read them, and at the end she prefers Dr Johnson.
seats.newValue: At first she says she has read them, and at the end she prefers Dr Johnson.
seats.execution: Lifts wording (line 9, line 49) without saying what changed. She prefers Dr Johnson in both answers; what differs is that line 14 still allows 'who knows what he may become', and line 49 gives the author nothing.

seats.oldValue: Explain that it is a different sort of thing.
seats.newValue: Tell madam it is quite a different sort of thing.
seats.execution: Line 18 is something he already said, 'It is quite a different sort of thing, my dear madam', not something he asks leave to do. The request is line 20: 'Just allow me to read you a scene'.

seats.oldValue: To let the Captain choose the second book.
seats.newValue: To let the Captain choose the second book to read.
seats.execution: The choosing belongs to Miss Jenkyns: at line 26 she orders 'Fetch me', naming the book herself, and at line 28 says 'Now allow _me_ to read you a scene'.

seats.oldValue: In a loud voice that the whole room could hear.
seats.newValue: In a loud voice that Miss Jenkyns surely heard.
seats.execution: Line 36 says he asked 'in a low voice', which the narrator thinks Miss Jenkyns 'could not have heard' (line 37). The text states the contrary of a loud voice she could not miss.

seats.oldValue: He agrees that those things were left out.
seats.newValue: He agrees that all of those things were left out.
seats.execution: Stuart says the plan 'doesn’t take into account' those delays (line 21); Fogg answers 'All included' (line 23), the opposite of agreeing they were left out.

seats.oldValue: The least possible time the journey can take.
seats.newValue: The least possible time for the journey.
seats.execution: Lines 50 to 51 say eighty days are 'the least possible time in which the journey can be made'. True inside the window, but it is the time, not the stake; what he will 'risk' is the twenty thousand at line 46.

seats.oldValue: She tells Jo to scold as much as she likes.
seats.newValue: Jo will never see her silly old book again.
seats.execution: True inside the window: line 15 has Amy say 'you’ll never see your silly old book again'. That is what follows, not what she has done; the deed is line 18, 'I burned it up.'

seats.oldValue: She tells her mother she will forgive Amy tomorrow.
seats.newValue: She tells her mother she will forgive Amy in the morning.
seats.execution: No such promise is in lines 39 to 43. She 'couldn’t quite forgive yet' (line 41) and says aloud that Amy 'doesn’t deserve to be forgiven' (lines 42 to 43).

seats.oldValue: She stamped her feet and blew on her fingers.
seats.newValue: She was stamping her feet and blowing on her fingers.
seats.execution: Line 64 gives the stamping and the blowing to Amy, 'stamping her feet and blowing on her fingers' as she put her skates on. They are moved onto Jo, who 'never turned' (line 65).

seats.oldValue: Angrily, after losing his temper with her.
seats.newValue: Angrily, as he could not keep his temper with her.
seats.execution: No temper is lost in lines 35 to 37. He asks 'in a low voice' (line 36), quiet enough that the narrator thinks Miss Jenkyns 'could not have heard' (line 37); anger is a likely-sounding manner the lines never give.

seats.oldValue: To be let past the hedge himself.
seats.newValue: The privilege of passing by the private road.
seats.execution: Reverses the exchange in lines 22 to 23. The rabbit asks 'Sixpence for the privilege of passing by the private road': the privilege is what the Mole would get, and the sixpence is what the rabbit wants from him.

seats.oldValue: To make the reader feel sorry for the Mole's sore arms.
seats.newValue: To make the reader feel sorry for the Mole's aching back.
seats.execution: Gives the effect of line 4, where he has 'an aching back and weary arms' from the cleaning, not of the repeated digging verbs in lines 11 to 13. Those make the climb itself feel long and hard.
